To seek Reinstatement or Appeal an enforcement action, fill out the Appeal and Reinstatement form [2]. You may appeal a moderation decision for up to six months following the decision, and GitHub may in its discretion refuse to consider appeals submitted more than six months after the decision [2]. GitHub staff review the information provided to determine whether there is sufficient information to warrant reinstatement or granting of the appeal [3].

GitHub may reverse or modify its decision when the appeal shows that (i) the decision to act or not act was mistaken, (ii) the content or conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with the Terms, or (iii) a lesser severity of action was warranted [7].

All appeal decisions are made by humans, not automated means; if the reviewing staff member is the same person who made the initial determination and would deny the appeal, a different staff member will independently review it [8]. All legitimate appeals are answered with a final decision [9]. If you believe a final appeal decision is still incorrect, you may in certain circumstances have additional rights under local law — for example, in the EU, possibly an out-of-court dispute settlement process under the Digital Services Act [10].

turns.question: Is all malware research code banned on GitHub?

facts: Dual-use research content can be allowed; do not assert a blanket ban.

response.answer:
No. The policy targets active abuse, not research content.

- GitHub prohibits using the platform in direct support of unlawful attacks that cause technical harms, e.g. delivering malicious executables or acting as attack infrastructure (DoS organization, command-and-control servers) [1].
- At the same time, GitHub explicitly allows dual-use content and supports posting content used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, because publishing it has educational value and benefits the security community [1].
- In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, GitHub may restrict that specific instance (typically behind authentication, with removal as a last resort), temporarily where feasible, without purging the content in perpetuity; there is an appeals process [1].
- Recommended (not required) steps for such repos: describe potentially harmful content in a README.md disclaimer, and provide an abuse-inquiry contact via SECURITY.md [1].
- Caveat: npm is treated as a platform primarily for installation and run-time use of code, not for research [1].

The general Acceptable Use Policies likewise ban directly supporting unlawful active attack or malware campaigns causing technical harms, with no dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring [2].

response.answer:
**No.** GitHub does not release, transfer, or reclaim usernames on the basis that they appear inactive or unused [1].

Key points:
- Account names are available on a first-come, first-served basis and are intended for immediate and active use [2].
- Not all activity is publicly visible, so accounts with no visible activity may still be in active use [3].
- If the name you want has already been claimed, you'll need to select a different available name — using a number, hyphen, or alternative spelling may help [4] — unless you are submitting a trademark complaint, as valid trademark-related complaints are the only requests reviewed for possible release of an already-claimed username [5].

Relatedly, GitHub prohibits account name squatting: names may not be reserved or inactively held for future use, and violating accounts may be removed or renamed without notice [6].

facts: Valid trademark complaints can be reviewed; transfer is not guaranteed.

response.answer:
Yes — a valid trademark complaint is the one route GitHub reviews for possibly releasing an already-claimed username [1].

- **Not automatic:** An account whose username happens to be the same as a registered trademark is not, by itself, necessarily a trademark policy violation [2], and usernames are first come, first served and may not be reserved [2].
- **What counts as a violation:** Using a company or business name, logo, or other trademark-protected materials in a manner that may mislead or confuse others about its brand or business affiliation may be considered a violation [3].
- **Possible outcomes:** For reports from holders of federal or international trademark registrations, GitHub reviews the account and may: suspend the account and notify the holder where there is a clear intent to mislead others [4]; or, where the account appears to confuse users but is not purposefully passing itself off as the trademarked good or service, give the account holder an opportunity to clear up confusion — and GitHub may also release the username for the trademark holder's active use [5].
- **Who can report and how:** Holders of registered trademarks can report via GitHub's trademark policy violation report form, using a company email address and clearly describing why the account may cause confusion with their mark or how it may dilute or tarnish it [6].

So the result depends on GitHub's review of confusion and intent; a transfer/release is a possibility, not a guarantee.

Note: A federal or international trademark registration number is required when reporting; if the reported name is not a registered mark (e.g., a government agency or non-profit), GitHub asks for identifying details instead [7].

Here's how to submit a moderation appeal to GitHub:

**How to submit**
If you seek Reinstatement or wish to appeal an enforcement action, you fill out GitHub's Appeal and Reinstatement form [1]. GitHub staff then review the information provided in the form to determine whether there is sufficient information to warrant reinstatement or granting the appeal [2].

**Deadline**
You may appeal a moderation decision for up to six months following the decision; GitHub may, in its discretion, refuse to consider appeals submitted more than six months after the decision [3].

**Appeal vs. Reinstatement**
- A **Reinstatement** applies where you wish to regain access to your account or content, are willing to make the necessary changes to address the violation, and agree not to violate the terms going forward [4].
- An **Appeal** applies where you dispute that a violation occurred and can provide additional information showing a different decision should have been reached [5].
- The form lets you explain your basis for disputing the decision and provide any additional information you believe should have led to a different decision [6].

**What to expect**
Decisions on appeal are made by humans, not automated means; if the reviewer was the same person who made the initial determination and would be inclined to deny the appeal, a different staff member reviews it independently [7]. All legitimate appeals will be answered with a final decision [8].

turns.question: Compare posting personal information with requesting removal of leaked access credentials.

facts: Distinguish the personal-information prohibition from the specific-risk removal process.

response.answer:
These are two sides of the same privacy topic, but different mechanisms: posting someone's personal information is a policy violation (a use restriction), while leaking access credentials is handled through a specific removal request process.

**Posting personal information (prohibited conduct)**
- GitHub does not allow content or activity that violates the privacy of a third party, such as posting another person's personal information without consent [1].
- The Doxxing and Invasion of Privacy policy says: don't post other people's personal information — including private email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses or other private location information, bank account/credit card numbers, Social Security/National Identity numbers, **passwords**, voter information, medical information and personal biometric data, and other private information that may pose a safety or security risk [2].
- Photos or videos taken or distributed without the subject's consent may also be considered an invasion of privacy, especially where they present a safety risk (e.g., intimidation or harassment) [3].
- Context matters, as does whether the content is publicly available elsewhere: sharing publicly available content may not itself violate the policy, but sharing it with intent to harass or incite abuse may violate the bullying and harassment prohibition [4].
- Notably, "passwords" appear on this doxxing list, so posting credentials can be a privacy violation too [2].

**Requesting removal of leaked access credentials (remedy process)**
- The Private Information Removal Policy is offered as an exceptional service only for high-risk content that violates the Terms of Service, such as when your security is at risk from exposed access credentials [5].
- "Private information" means content that (i) should have been kept confidential and (ii) whose public availability poses a specific or targeted security risk; "security risk" means exposure to physical danger, identity theft, or increased likelihood of unauthorized access to physical or network facilities [6].
- Requests are appropriate for access credentials such as usernames with passwords, access tokens or other sensitive secrets granting access to your organization's server, network or domain, and for AWS tokens or similar credentials granting third-party access on your behalf — where you must be able to show the token belongs to you [7].
- The process is not for internal server names/IPs/URLs on their own, mere mentions of your company, whole files or repositories without a specific security risk, copyright (use the DMCA Takedown Policy), trademark (use the Trademark Policy), or privacy complaints about your own account data (use the privacy contact form) [8].
- It is not used for other content categories, and private-information requests should be sent separately from infringement requests so they aren't processed simultaneously [9].
- Requirements: a working clickable link to each file (not search results, examples or screenshots), specific line numbers, a description of how each item poses a security risk beyond merely asserting it, and — if acting as an agent — a statement that you have a legal right to act on behalf of the organization; optionally flag urgency such as a very recent credential exposure [10].
- Process: GitHub generally contacts the repository user first to let them delete/modify the information or dispute the claim; if they don't respond within the allowed window, GitHub will disable the repository [11]. Forks are not automatically disabled, and requesters must expressly include them [12].

**Key comparison:** The doxxing rule is a conduct prohibition with no listed filing requirements, enforced by reporting abuse and evaluated on context/public availability [4]. The credential-removal path is a narrowly scoped, high-risk-only service with strict evidentiary requirements (exact file links, line numbers, security-risk explanation, ownership proof) and a user-notice/dispute workflow [5][7][10][11].

facts: DMCA handles copyright; trademark reports use a separate process.

response.answer:
No — a DMCA notice is the copyright route; trademark complaints go through GitHub's separate Trademark Policy [1]. Each category has its own reporting requirements, and incomplete reports get sent back for clarification or revision [2]. GitHub also says it can't tell you which policy fits your situation and recommends independent legal counsel if you're unsure [3].

Required information includes the username, company name, company website, the mark, registration number and registration office (e.g., USPTO), a description of the confusion, and the requested action, plus the good-faith, perjury, and signature statements [7]. A federal or international registration number is required, with an alternative information set for names that are not registered marks (e.g., government agencies or non-profits) [8]. GitHub may suspend an account for clear intent to mislead, or, where confusion appears unintentional, give the account holder a chance to clear it up and possibly release the username [9].

response.answer:
Yes on both counts.

**Research:** GitHub allows dual-use content and supports posting content used for research into vulnerabilities, malware, or exploits, because publication/distribution has educational value and a net benefit to the security community; GitHub assumes positive intention [1]. The bar on "technical harms" (resource overconsumption, physical damage, downtime, denial of service, data loss) applies with no implicit or explicit dual-use purpose prior to the abuse occurring [2]. In rare cases of very widespread abuse of dual-use content, GitHub may restrict access to that specific instance to disrupt an ongoing unlawful attack or malware campaign — usually by putting the content behind authentication, or as an option of last resort by disabling access or full removal (e.g., when posted as a gist) — and will contact project owners where possible [3]. Restrictions are temporary where feasible and are not meant to purge dual-use content in perpetuity; if you feel your content was unduly restricted, there is an appeals process [4]. Note GitHub considers the npm registry a platform primarily for installation and run-time use of code, not for research [5].

**Appeal:** An "Appeal" is where you dispute that a violation occurred and provide additional information showing a different decision should have been reached [6]. You submit it via the Appeal and Reinstatement form, and you may appeal a moderation decision for up to six months following the decision; GitHub may in its discretion refuse to consider appeals submitted later than six months [7]. GitHub will reverse or modify its decision when the appeal shows (i) the decision was mistaken; (ii) the content or conduct was not illegal and not incompatible with the Terms; or (iii) a lesser severity of action is warranted [8]. All appeal decisions are made by humans, not automated means, and a reviewer who made the initial determination and would deny the appeal is replaced by a different independent staff member [9]. All legitimate appeals will be answered with a final decision [10].

For future posts, GitHub recommends (but does not require) clearly identifying potentially harmful content in a README disclaimer or source comments, and providing a contact method (e.g., SECURITY.md) for third-party abuse inquiries [11].

I can't tell you the outcome for your specific restriction; the above is the process for raising it.

turns.question: Are forks automatically removed for either copyright or private-information takedowns?

facts: Neither process automatically removes every fork; acknowledge investigation and specified exceptions.

response.answer:
No — in both processes, forks are not automatically disabled.

**Copyright (DMCA):** GitHub *will not* automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository, because forks belong to different users, may have been altered in significant ways, and may be licensed or used in a different way protected by fair use; GitHub does not conduct any independent investigation into forks [1]. If at the time the notice was submitted all existing forks of that repository were identified as allegedly infringing, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in that network at the time the notice is processed, and if the reported network is larger than 100 repositories it may consider disabling the entire network if the notice states the specified sworn language [2].

**Private information:** GitHub likewise will not automatically disable forks when disabling a parent repository, since forks belong to different users and may have been altered in significant ways, and GitHub does not independently investigate forks — requesters must expressly include forks in their request [3]. If all existing forks were identified at the time of the notice, GitHub would process a valid claim against all forks in that network, and for networks larger than 100 repositories it may consider disabling the entire network if the notice states that, based on the representative number of forks reviewed, all or most forks are believed to contain the reported content [4].

citations.content: GitHub provides [a number of account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials) including an [automated recovery process](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials#authenticating-with-a-verified-device-ssh-token-or-personal-access-token) if you have lost access to your GitHub.com account. **If you cannot use any of the provided recovery methods, you have permanently lost access to your account.**

citations.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
citations.content: For security reasons, **GitHub Support will not restore access to accounts with two-factor authentication enabled if you lose your two-factor authentication credentials or lose access to your account recovery methods.** You must use existing [account recovery methods](/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/recovering-your-account-if-you-lose-your-2fa-credentials).

citations.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
citations.content: GitHub does not support any other means of account recovery, including social or ID verification, by members of GitHub’s staff. This policy is in place to protect your account from unauthorized access through social engineering.

citations.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
citations.content: You can, however, [unlink email addresses](/account-and-profile/setting-up-and-managing-your-personal-account-on-github/managing-your-personal-account/unlinking-your-email-address-from-a-locked-account) from a locked account in order to create a new account or use the email on another existing account.

citations.title: GitHub Account Recovery Policy
citations.content:
If you have lost access to a user account, you may [clone](/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/cloning-a-repository) or [fork](/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/fork-a-repo) any content that is public.

If you have lost access to an organization account, you may clone or fork any content that is public and you may be able to request that remaining members of the organization clone or fork any private content.

GitHub Support will not recover the contents of a user or organization account that is locked.
